segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Over the years, attitudes towards workers have changed considerably.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: After all, there was a time when workers had no rights at all, and laboured in appalling conditions.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Conditions have improved a lot, but conflict in the workplace is still common.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: And human resources managers nowadays need to be able to deal with it when necessary.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: What is conflict in the workplace?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Definitions vary, but I’m taking it to refer to a whole range of behaviours that the victim finds unacceptable, from minor, harmless arguments to – at the opposite extreme – physical violence.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Much of this is covered by the term bullying, by which I mean one or more people behaving abusively or aggressively against another who is in a weaker position.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Although all behaviour like this is a form of conflict, not all conflict can be described in these terms.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: As with all human behaviour, there are numerous reasons for it.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But often it’s caused by someone who feels the need to show their superiority over someone else, in order to feel that they aren’t at the lowest level in a hierarchy or a group of people.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: In some cases one person simply dislikes the other, on the basis that the personality of one is in some way incompatible with that of the other person.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: A general habit of optimism in one person could make them intolerant of a colleague who’s constantly pessimistic – not that that justifies treating them badly, of course.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Some conflicts arise when people are more interested in promoting themselves and their team than in the company as a whole.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: These conflicts are called ‘structural’, and could come about, for example, when a sales team believe they are the only people in the business who do any useful work, and look down on behind-the-scenes administrators.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Conflict obviously affects the individuals concerned – the situation is likely to be very stressful for victims, resulting in their absence from work, possibly for months.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: For the company, if no effort is made to deal with conflict, it can spiral out of control, and even lead to the breakdown of the business.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Some interesting work with chief executives – CEOs – has uncovered some of the reasons why they may treat colleagues badly.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Many CEOs combine two opposing characteristics: confidence – that is, the belief that they’re capable of great achievements – with a high level of anxiety, a fear of missing targets, whether set by themselves or by the directors of the company.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This combination can make them respond badly to anyone who questions their decisions.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: In a high pressure work environment, such characteristics become problematic.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: And it’s particularly difficult to tackle the situation where colleagues, managers and board members are all trying to achieve their own visions.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: When they can’t agree on strategic issues and on where they see the business going, there are real problems. For managers at lower levels within the organisation, it might seem that an autocratic form of management – where the chief executive gives orders and everyone else has to obey – would see more conflict than others.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Interestingly, though, a company with a more democratic business model, can suffer more, when uncertainty about who to report to leads to conflicting demands. Now I’ll say a little about dealing with the type of conflict that has harmful effects.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Of course the ideal is to prevent it arising in the first place.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: A good manager, at any level, will make efforts to earn the respect of the people they work with, particularly those who report to them.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: That will involve politeness in all communications, and treating them as equals who happen to have a different role within the organisation.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Sometimes, of course, conflict does occur, and can get out of hand.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: In such cases the human resources department often gets involved.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: However, if one of the parties in a conflict sees human resources as simply a mouthpiece for the chief executive, then an external mediator might be able to help.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: By talking to both sides, and trying to find the truth of what’s been happening, they can build a clear picture of the situation, and give feedback that both sides will accept, precisely because they’re independent.
